lead: On this Friday of Lent the readings look at where the heart is now. Ezekiel tells a discouraged people that no one is trapped by the past, neither the sinner by his sins nor the good man by his good record. Jesus takes the commandment against murder down to its root in anger, and then sends us away from the altar to make peace. The key words are turn, live and be reconciled.

r.h: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked?
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first deportation of 597 BC (1:1–3). Jerusalem was then destroyed in 587. Among the exiles a bitter saying went round: “The parents have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (18:2). It meant: we are paying for our ancestors’ sins, and nothing we do can matter.

Chapter 18 answers that saying. Each person stands before God on his own account, and the present turning of a life counts. Scripture also knows of the way sin harms later generations, and Ezekiel does not deny that. He is speaking to a despair that was using it as an excuse. The words “live” and “die” here mean life and death under God’s covenant, in a time when belief in life after death had not yet become clear.
str: vv. 21–22: the wicked who turn shall live.
v. 23: the central question from God.
v. 24: the righteous who turn away.
vv. 25–28: “The way of the Lord is unfair”: God’s answer, and the same two cases once more.
kw: As so often in the prophets, this is the word for conversion. It runs right through the chapter and appears in both directions: away from sin, and away from righteousness.
The word is used of what someone really delights in. God’s own question denies that he delights in the sinner’s death. Ezekiel 33:11 repeats it on God’s oath.
From a verb meaning to weigh or to measure. The people say God’s scales are not true. God turns the charge back to them (v. 25).
vv: None of the transgressions that they have committed shall be remembered against them;
The past really is past. This is the Old Testament’s strong word for what the Church offers in the sacrament of Penance.
Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?
This is the heart of the reading, and it comes as a question because God wants us to answer it. God “desires everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4).
Yet you say, “The way of the Lord is unfair.”
It is a very human complaint. It may be heard from the elder brother in the parable of the prodigal son. God’s mercy can look unfair to those who keep accounts.
Because they considered and turned away from all the transgressions that they had committed, they shall surely live; they shall not die.
The verb “considered” is worth noticing. Conversion begins when a person stops, looks honestly at his life, and sees it.
ch: The Church hears in this passage both her hope and her warning. Mortal sin, if not redeemed by repentance and God’s forgiveness, leads to exclusion from Christ’s kingdom; but we must entrust judgment of persons to God’s mercy (CCC 1861). God wills no one to perish, and desires all to come to repentance (CCC 1037; 2 Peter 3:9). Lent is the Church’s time for this “consider and turn”, and the sacrament of Penance is its proper place (CCC 1422–1424).

set: Jesus has just said that he came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it (5:17–19). Verse 20 is the heading for what follows, and vv. 21–48 give six examples, each with “You have heard… But I say to you”. Today’s is the first, on murder.

Jesus’ word about the scribes and Pharisees is not an attack on the Jewish people or on the Law. The Pharisees’ own concern for keeping the Law in spirit as well as letter was close to his own (CCC 579). Many scholars think that Matthew writes in a time of tension between his community and other Jewish teachers, and a reader should keep that in mind. Jesus asks his disciples for a righteousness that goes to the root.
str: v. 20: the heading: a greater righteousness.
vv. 21–22: from murder to anger and insult.
vv. 23–24: first example: at the altar.
vv. 25–26: second example: on the way to court.
kw: In Matthew, doing God’s will as a response to his grace: right relations with God and with others. It is a key word of the Sermon on the Mount.
From the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). In later Jewish writing and in the Gospels the name is used for final punishment.
The only use of this verb in the New Testament. It is a command, and notice whose duty it is: the one who remembers that the other has something against him.
vv: But I say to you that if you are angry with a brother or sister, you will be liable to judgment;

A note on the text. Many later manuscripts add “without cause”; the oldest do not have it, and neither does the NRSV. The rising list (anger, an insult, “You fool”) is not a table of penalties. It is a way of saying that murder begins here. The word the NRSV renders “insult” is the Aramaic raka, “empty-head”.
So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you,
Note that it is not “if you have something against him”. Even if the fault is the other’s, the first step falls to me.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
For a Galilean the altar was days away in Jerusalem, and that is part of the force of the picture. Jesus is not setting worship aside. “Then come”: he wants the gift, from a reconciled heart.
Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are on the way to court with him,
There is an urgency. There is still time on the road. A quarrel left alone grows, and so does its cost.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Lord adds to “You shall not kill” the proscription of anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262), and that from the Sermon on the Mount onward he insists on conversion of heart, reconciliation with one’s brother before presenting an offering on the altar (CCC 2608). The very old Didache tells Christians at odds with one another not to join the Sunday Eucharist until they are reconciled, so that the sacrifice may not be defiled (in substance; ch. 14). At Mass the Sign of Peace keeps this teaching before us.

qa: Does one sin wipe out a whole good life, as Ezekiel seems to say?

Ezekiel is describing a change in the direction of a life, “turning away” and doing the abominable things of the wicked, not a slip. The Church distinguishes mortal and venial sin (CCC 1854–1855). One mortal sin does lose the state of grace (CCC 1861), yet even a grave sin is not the end, since the same chapter that warns the righteous also promises life to anyone who turns back. What the prophet refuses is the idea that a good record is a bank account against which one may sin.
study: Do I think of myself as trapped by my past, or as safe because of my good record? What does Ezekiel say to me?
Who has something against me? What one step could I take before my next Communion?
